CLASS 35 · AGES 4–5 · 20 COUNTING LESSONS

Numbers, Counting & Early Math.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Twenty numbers, one smiling fruit at a time.

Every number in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: open the counting card together, count the smiling fruit, say the number, follow the teaching steps, ask the questions and finish with something real to count in your own kitchen. The order is gentle: cards one to five fit on one hand, cards six to ten need both hands, and the teens repeat one quiet pattern — a full ten, plus some more.

One card a sitting is plenty; the whole class is a month of two-minute counting moments. The kitchen is the answer key, so practice arrives with every snack — and reaching twenty earns a celebration the whole family can hear.

MEASURE, COUNT, SPEND

Class 42 · Measuring & Money.

Class 35 counts from one apple to twenty figs — and the Measuring & Money class puts those numbers to work: twenty-eight printable math cards for ages 4–5 with number bonds, tens and ones, odd and even, adding groups, taking away, measuring with a ruler and a balance, and counting out coins, price and change. Every card downloads and prints straight from the class page with its rule and a way to try it today right beneath the image.

FROM COUNTING CARDS TO REAL SUMS

Class 46 · Early Addition & Subtraction.

Class 35 counts from one apple to twenty figs — and the Early Addition & Subtraction class is where those numbers finally meet a plus sign. Thirty printable math flashcards for ages 4–5, every card on the one class page, every answer left blank for your child to count out on real things.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 20 cards in Numbers, Counting & Early Math, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Numbers, Counting & Early Math. We have 20 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. 02
    Card 1 · One Apple

    “One apple. Just one — can you find one of something nearby?”

    How: Hand your child one of something real — one biscuit, one spoon, one shoe — and wait for them to announce the number. One feels powerful when it is claimed out loud.

  3. 03
    Card 2 · Two Bananas

    “Two bananas — one, two. What else comes in twos?”

    How: Hunt for pairs around the room: two shoes, two ears, two sleeves. Touch each one as you count it, left then right, so the pair gets counted twice on purpose and once on purpose again.

  4. 04
    Card 3 · Three Oranges

    “One, two, three oranges. Let us find three of something.”

    How: Play the three-game at snack time: three orange segments, three crackers, three sips of water — count each one into the plate before the first bite happens.

  5. 05
    Card 4 · Four Strawberries

    “Four strawberries. How many legs does our table have?”

    How: Crouch under the table and count the legs together — one, two, three, four. Then count the dog or teddy's paws. Four keeps turning up, and finding it twice makes it stick.

  6. 06
    Card 5 · Five Pears

    “Five pears — and look, five fingers on one hand.”

    How: Hold up one hand and count the fingers slowly, tapping each one. Then press the whole hand flat on the card and say "five" for the match. Hand and number become the same thing.

  7. 07
    Card 6 · Six Grapes

    “Six grapes — more than one hand can hold.”

    How: Line up six snack grapes in two rows of three, exactly like the card, and count them. Then eat one and count again. Five is not a failure; it is the next question.

  8. 08
    Card 7 · Seven Cherries

    “Seven cherries — and seven days in our week.”

    How: Count the seven days of the week out loud on your fingers, one finger per day. Then count the cherries the same way. Two sevens for the price of one card.

  9. 09
    Card 8 · Eight Watermelons

    “Eight slices — the 8 looks like two circles, one on top of the other.”

    How: Cut or break a snack into eight pieces, lay them out like the card and count before eating. An octopus with eight arms makes a fine count-along friend too.

  10. 10
    Card 9 · Nine Peaches

    “Nine peaches — one shy of ten.”

    How: Count nine steps down the hallway, then turn around and count nine back. Add one more step at the door and let your child discover what ten feels like.

  11. 11
    Card 10 · Ten Blueberries

    “Ten blueberries — all the fingers on both hands.”

    How: Count all ten fingers, left hand then right. Then count the berries row by row — five and five make ten. Two hands, two rows, one number: that is the whole trick of ten.

  12. 12
    Card 11 · Eleven Kiwis

    “Eleven — that is ten kiwis and one more.”

    How: Count out ten blocks or berries in a row, then add one more and say "eleven" at the newcomer. Ten-plus-one is the entire secret of the teens, learned with a snack.

  13. 13
    Card 12 · Twelve Lemons

    “Twelve lemons — a whole dozen.”

    How: Hunt for twelve at home: a dozen eggs in the box, twelve months on the calendar, twelve numbers on a clock. Say "dozen" each time — a real grown-up word, earned.

  14. 14
    Card 13 · Thirteen Pineapples

    “Thir-TEEN. A funny word — let us say it slowly.”

    How: Count thirteen stairs together, one word per step. Stairs slow the voice down, and thirteen said thirteen times on real steps stops being a tongue trap.

  15. 15
    Card 14 · Fourteen Raspberries

    “Fourteen — ten raspberries and four more.”

    How: Count out ten of anything, then four more beside them, and say the two groups out loud: ten and four make fourteen. A fortnight is two weeks — fourteen days — if the word comes up.

  16. 16
    Card 15 · Fifteen Mangoes

    “Fifteen — ten and five more.”

    How: Count all ten fingers, then all ten toes, then just five toes on one foot: ten fingers and five toes are fifteen. Wiggling toes while counting is allowed and encouraged.

  17. 17
    Card 16 · Sixteen Coconuts

    “Sixteen — ten coconuts and six more.”

    How: Build a square of sixteen blocks, four rows of four, and count the sides. Then count all sixteen. The same number, two shapes — squares and rows are both true.

  18. 18
    Card 17 · Seventeen Apples

    “Seventeen — ten apples, then seven more.”

    How: Clap-count to seventeen, one clap per number, with the voice staying as steady as the hands. If the count tangles near the end, shrug and climb again from ten.

  19. 19
    Card 18 · Eighteen Bananas

    “Eighteen — ten bananas and eight more.”

    How: Sort a pile of small coins or buttons into two rows of nine and count them all: eighteen. Rows make big numbers feel manageable, and sorting them is half the fun.

  20. 20
    Card 19 · Nineteen Apricots

    “Nineteen — one away from twenty.”

    How: Count nineteen slowly, then pause dramatically and ask what comes next. The "twenty!" that gets shouted back should be celebrated like a goal scored.

  21. 21
    Card 20 · Twenty Figs

    “Twenty figs — two rows of ten, or four rows of five. Same twenty.”

    How: Count the twenty figs row by row, then cover one row of five and count what is left. Uncover, count again. Twenty can be taken apart and rebuilt, and that is the whole point.

  22. 22
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  23. 23
    Check

    “Can you find One Apple? Now show me Eleven Kiwis.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  24. 24
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 20 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
